name: Chloe Torres

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I buy garden and pet supplies for Meadowbrook Wholesale: compost, bird seed, dog beds, fish food, you name it. We sell to about 150 garden centres, so my year runs on the weather, and spring is madness. I came over from a garden centre till seven years ago and I'm still the junior on a team of four. I love a good price on a pallet of bulbs, and I hate it when a cold April leaves us sitting on thousands of unsold hose reels.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AI Plateau". Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, because a calm world is easier to plan for. At work I'd tell the team it's a useful assistant and not a miracle, and I'd probably show somebody a trick over lunch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'm fine. I use an AI assistant every day to read the weather outlook and last year's sales and suggest order sizes. My manager Yvonne likes my numbers, and we've got about four months saved, so no big worries.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and tinker a bit more. I'd ask Yvonne if I can run the tool on the bird seed range as a trial, and I'd keep the 150 pounds a month going into the savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, honestly. A bit bored, even. I like it when the world is easy to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the AI tool actually help with the weather problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It reads the long-range forecast and last year's till data for the garden centres, then gives me a first guess for how many compost bags and hose reels to buy. I adjust it, because my tool doesn't know that Mr Kowalski, a garden centre owner, always panic-buys in March.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your partner Marco make of your using it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco's an electrician and he thinks it's brilliant, until it's his own trade. He says wiring needs hands and a head, and he's happy to say that to anyone. But he laughs that I talk to my laptop more than to him.

say: I'd say a calm world is **easier** to plan for.
I'd tell the team it's a useful **assistant**, not a miracle.
think: I'm fine: I use an AI assistant **daily** and Yvonne likes my numbers.
We have about four months **saved**, so no big worries.
do: Ask Yvonne to run the tool on the **bird seed** range as a trial.
Keep **150 pounds** a month going into savings.
feel: **Calm**, a bit bored; I like a world that's easy to plan for.
S0.quote: My tool doesn't know that Mr Kowalski, a garden centre owner, always panic-buys in March.
fieldNote: Already a **daily user** with real results.
Uses the tool for a first **guess**, adjusting with local knowledge.
Calm is backed by **savings** and a manager who likes her work.

steps.text: Trial the AI order tool on the bird seed range
Keep refining my weather and sales prompts each week
Put 150 pounds a month into savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "Steady Disruption". Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and mostly a useful one, but people need help getting there. At work I'd offer to run a lunchtime session for the older buyers who haven't tried it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'm a little uneasy. If the tool does my guesswork, there's a day when Yvonne asks why there are four of us. I'm the junior with seven years in, and I know that matters.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd make myself the person who knows the tool best. I'd build a proper ordering process around it, write down how it works, and ask for a raise for doing it. I'd also keep a list of the garden centres who know me by name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but also a little thrilled. It's like being on a boat that's starting to move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the tool can do your buying, what is the human part of the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The human part is the weird orders, the new suppliers, and ringing a garden centre owner when a delivery's gone wrong. Nobody wants to hear a chatbot apologise. I'd say that's maybe half the job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle the others on the team who don't use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd help them, honestly. A team that all uses it is harder to cut one by one. If I show Gordon how to use it, he'll keep his job longer, and that's good for me too.

say: I'd say it's a big, mostly **useful** change that needs help getting there.
I'd offer a **lunchtime session** for buyers who haven't tried it.
think: If the tool does my guesswork, Yvonne may ask why there are **four** of us.
With seven years in, I'm still the **junior**, and it matters.
do: Make myself the person who knows the tool **best** and write down how it works.
Ask for a **raise** and keep a list of garden centres who know me.
feel: **Uneasy** but a little thrilled, like a boat starting to move.
S1.quote: Nobody wants to hear a chatbot apologise.
fieldNote: Uses **strategy**: spreads skills so the team can't be cut one by one.
Knows the **human half** of the job is calling customers.
Enjoys the **change** as well as fearing it.

steps.text: Run a lunchtime AI session for the older buyers
Write down the AI ordering process step by step
Ask Yvonne for a pay review for running the tool

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2028". Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got to be sensible, and quick. I'd tell friends this isn't a thing to joke about, and that the boring plans, like savings and skills, are what matter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the desk jobs go first and fast, and mine is one of them. Within two years, I'd say Meadowbrook buys with a few people, and a junior of 58 isn't one of those few.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd work on two things. First, I'd get as good as I can with the AI tools so I'm useful for as long as possible. Second, I'd call the garden centres I know and ask what they'd need, because maybe I can be their contact, not Meadowbrook's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Properly worried, and trying to look cheerful at home. Marco knows, but I don't say it out loud at dinner.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marco's work mean for you two, with the three extra years for robots?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Marco's an electrician, so robots reach his work about 2031. That gives us extra years, and for those years his wage is the main one. We'd have to live on it, and on savings, until that changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is your fallback if the buying team is gone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd become a freelance buying adviser for small garden centres, using AI to do the clever bit and charging a modest fee. It's not a certainty, but it plays to what I know, and it uses the tool I'm already good with.

say: I'd say we must be **sensible and quick**.
I'd say boring plans, savings and skills, are what **matter**.
think: Desk jobs go first and **fast**, and mine is one of them.
A **58-year-old** junior isn't one of the few Meadowbrook would keep.
do: Get as good as I can with **AI tools** to stay useful.
Call garden centres I know about becoming their **buying contact**.
feel: **Worried**, and trying to look cheerful at home.
S2.quote: My partner Marco's an electrician, so robots reach his work about 2031. That gives us extra years, and for those years his wage is the main one.
fieldNote: Thinks clearly about **timing**: desk first, Marco's trade later.
Imagines a **freelance** buying adviser role built on tools she already uses.
Hides her **worry** at the dinner table.

steps.text: Practise AI buying tools until I can teach them
Offer paid buying advice to small garden centres
Ask garden centre owners I know about a supplier contact role

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2031". Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means we're all fine if we get on with it. I'd tell the team to treat the next year as a training year, and that the ones who start early will end up setting the rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be a bit calmer. At 63 I'd have time to build the advice side, and Marco would be working. I'd say it's a bit scary and a bit of an opportunity.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd take an evening course in small business accounts and sign up two garden centres as paying customers. I'd keep Meadowbrook going as long as they'd have me, then cut my hours to three days when the advice work is up to 600 pounds a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but hopeful. I'd say the hopeful part is bigger than I expected.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What do you do in the first year, that you wouldn't do with two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money part, honestly. I've never invoiced anyone. I've always had a pay slip. But I've got four months saved and Marco's income, so a slow start is survivable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about running your own advice business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut it down to the garden centres I've known for ten years and stay small. I'd rather have six loyal clients than sixty strangers.

say: I'd tell the team to treat the next year as a **training year**.
I'd say the ones who start early will **set the rules**.
think: At 63 I'd have time to build the **advice side**.
Marco would still be **working**, so it's scary but also an opportunity.
do: Take an evening course in **small business accounts** at the college.
Sign up two garden centres as **paying customers** within the first year.
feel: **Uneasy but hopeful**; the hopeful part is bigger than I expected.
S3.quote: I'd rather have six loyal clients than sixty strangers.
fieldNote: Plans in **numbers**: two clients in year one, 600 pounds a month.
Has never **invoiced** anyone and says so.
Keeps the dream **small** and tied to relationships she already has.

steps.text: Take an evening course in small business accounts
Sign two garden centres as paying clients in year one
Cut Meadowbrook to three days once advice hits 600 pounds

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called "AGI by 2036". Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time to prepare, so people shouldn't say they weren't warned. I'd tell my younger colleagues to take it seriously, but not to be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I'd be 68 and long retired, so it won't land on my own desk. I'd be thinking more about my nephew Rafa, who's just starting out in the garden trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to about 65, using the tools, and keep the advice side as a pleasant extra. I'd save up to about six months, and then enjoy a bit of travel with Marco.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A tiny bit guilty, since I'm lucky with the timing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does a ten year warning make you take it less seriously?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take it seriously, but not in a gloomy way. The tools will change a lot in ten years, and the best thing is to keep playing with them. I'd just keep in practice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with the time off if you retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Walk the dogs, do the garden, finally take that trip to Portugal with Marco. I'd teach an AI class to the over-sixties at the library, because I love showing people.

say: I'd say ten years is a **long time** to prepare, so no one can say they weren't warned.
I'd tell younger colleagues to take it seriously but not be **scared**.
think: I'd be **68** and long retired, so it won't land on my own desk.
I'd think more about my nephew Rafa, just starting in the **garden trade**.
do: Keep working to about **65** and use the tools.
Save up to **six months** and travel with Marco.
feel: **Calm**, a tiny bit guilty about lucky timing.
S4.quote: I'd teach an AI class to the over-sixties at the library, because I love showing people.
fieldNote: Sees the longer timeline as **luck**, not safety.
Imagines **teaching** others as a retirement role.
Worries about her nephew, a **younger worker**, more than she worries about herself.

steps.text: Keep buying at Meadowbrook until I'm 65
Build savings to six months before retiring
Advise my nephew Rafa on garden trade careers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two year one, because I'd be 60 with a buying team that might not exist and only four months saved. What would help is the freedom to try something of my own, and some public support for people my age while we learn it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptive at 58 isn't the same as being safe. I use the tools every day, and I still know that someone younger and cheaper can learn them in a month.

headlineQuote: Being adaptive at 58 isn't the same as being safe.
portrait: Chloe is a **58-year-old** junior buyer of garden and pet supplies who still feels like the new one after seven years.
She uses AI **every day** to read weather and sales data and has real results to show.
Centre in outlook, she is practical and **chatty**, and wants to help her team learn too.
Her husband Marco is a **self-employed electrician**, and the household has about four months saved.
Her mood stays between calm and uneasy, with a plan to become a **freelance buying adviser**.
biggestWorry: The **two year** picture, with the buying team gone and just four months saved.
whatWouldHelp: The freedom to try something **of her own** and public support for older workers while they learn.
